transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you in today?

Well, doc, it’s... it’s hard to put into words exactly, but I just don’t feel like myself anymore. I really don't. I mean, I’ve been working as a janitor over at the community college for going on fifteen years now, and usually, you know, I’d chat with the night staff or at least wave to the security guys, maybe make a little small talk about the weather or the sports scores. But lately? I just... I barely talk to anyone. I don't want to. I just go completely flat, you know? Like all the air has been let out of my tires. I’m just quiet. And it’s not just the talking, it’s the work itself. I used to just grab my cart and go, get into a rhythm with the sweeping and the mopping, but now... man, even just getting started on my cleaning route feels like I’m pushing a loaded cart uphill through mud. Every single night, it’s just this huge, exhausting effort to even lift a mop or empty a trash can. It’s like my battery is just dead, and no matter what I do, it won't charge back up. I just feel so empty and stuck, and it’s really starting to mess with my job and my life.
Have you noticed that you don’t enjoy things as much as you used to, even activities that used to bring you some pleasure or satisfaction?

Well, yeah, that’s exactly it. It’s like... everything’s just gray now. I used to really look forward to my Saturdays, you know? I’d get up early, before the sun was even fully up, and head out to the lake for some fishing. I had this spot, right by the old willow tree, where the bass would always bite if you hit it just right in the morning. And even if they didn't bite, it was just nice being out there, listening to the water. Or even just the simple things, like sitting down with a hot cup of coffee and the Sunday crossword puzzle. I used to finish those things in pen, if you can believe it. I loved the challenge of it. 

And at work, too. I mean, I know it’s just cleaning, but I took pride in it. I used to show the younger guys, the new hires, all the little tricks I’ve learned over the years. Like the best way to strip a floor without leaving those awful swirl marks, or how to get the scuffs out of the baseboards without breaking your back. It felt good to pass that on, to see them get it. But now? Now I just... I let all of it sit. My fishing gear is just gathering dust in the garage, I haven't even looked at a crossword in months, and at work, I just keep my head down. I don't even try to talk to the new guys anymore. It’s just... none of it gives me anything back anymore. There’s no spark, no satisfaction. It’s all just another chore I don't have the energy for.
Have you been feeling down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, for the past couple of weeks?

I mean... depressed? I don't know if that's the right word for it. And as for every single day, or if it's been exactly a couple of weeks... I honestly couldn't tell you. Time just sort of bleeds together on the night shift anyway, you know? Like, I'll be sitting in the breakroom—we have this little room down in the basement of the science building, right next to the boiler room, so there's always this low, rumbling hum in the background. I'll just sit there on my fifteen-minute break, staring at the glass on the vending machine. The route guy, he usually restocks it on Thursdays, always wears this bright blue polo shirt, and he used to always ask how my night was going. Now I just kind of nod at him. I don't even care about getting a coffee or a pack of peanuts anymore. 

I just sit there under those buzzing fluorescent lights, and I don't feel sad, like crying sad, you know? Just... heavy. Like I was saying before. So I don't know if that counts as being down most of the day, or if it's been two weeks or five weeks. My supervisor, Gary, he was asking me just the other night if I was feeling alright because I didn't laugh at his joke—he always tells these terrible, cheesy jokes when we clock in—and I just looked at him. I couldn't even muster up the energy to fake a chuckle for the guy. But is that depressed? I don't really know. It's just this constant... nothingness, I guess. I'm not sure if that answers your question, doc, but I just don't keep track of the days like I used to.
Over the past two weeks, have you felt unusually tired or noticed a decrease in your energy levels almost every day?

Tired... yeah, I guess you could say that. But it’s not just a normal kind of tired, doc. It’s... well, let me put it this way. I’ll actually get a full night of sleep, right? I'll go to bed, sleep all the way through the day—since I work the night shift, you know—and I'll get a solid seven or eight hours. I'll wake up, have my coffee, and get in my truck to drive to the campus. It’s only about a fifteen, maybe twenty-minute drive down Route 9, depending on if you hit the lights right. 

But by the time I pull into the staff parking lot, right behind the humanities building, and put the truck in park... I go to open the door, and my arms and legs just feel so heavy. Like they're made of wet cement. And I haven't even clocked in yet! I haven't even walked down to the basement to see Gary or picked up a broom, and I already feel like I've worked a double shift. 

And then, when I actually start my route... I mean, I've been doing this for fifteen years, my body knows the motions. But lately, even the really small jobs just completely wear me out way more than they ever should. Take the trash bags, for instance. Over in the main concourse, we have these standard bins, and usually, you just tie off the plastic, heave it up, and toss it into the rolling bin. Simple, right? You don't even think about it, you just do it and move on to the next one. But now, I go to haul just one or two of those bags, and it takes everything out of me. I'll be standing there by the bin, leaning on the rim, just completely wiped out from lifting a few pounds of paper cups and wrappers. It’s like my muscles just quit on me, even if I did nothing but sleep before I got there. So yeah, I guess my energy is just... it's just completely gone.
Have you completely lost interest in doing things you used to enjoy, like fishing or working with the new hires at your job?

Well, yeah, I mean... I think I kind of mentioned this earlier, doc, but yeah, it's just exactly like that. I really have completely lost interest in all of it. Like I was saying about the fishing... I used to genuinely look forward to those Saturday mornings. I'd have my thermos of coffee, the old green one with the dent in the side from when I dropped it on the rocks back in '98, and I'd just sit out there by the willow tree. It was peaceful. I felt connected to something, you know? And the crossword puzzles, too. Sitting at the kitchen table, the Sunday paper spread out, trying to figure out a seven-letter word for 'obsolete' while the sun came through the window... I loved it. 

And work... I know it sounds silly, being a janitor and all, but I liked showing the new guys the ropes. I liked feeling useful, passing down those little tricks for stripping a floor without leaving the swirl marks, or getting the scuffs off the baseboards. I felt like I was contributing, like my fifteen years of doing this meant something to somebody. 

But now... I don't know, doc. I really just let all of those things sit. The fishing rods are in the corner of the garage, probably covered in spider webs by now. I haven't bought a Sunday paper in months. And at work, I just... I don't even bother with the new hires. I see them struggling with the buffer machine, making a mess of the wax, and I just walk right past them. I just don't care. None of it gives me anything back anymore. There's no joy in it, no satisfaction, no... nothing. It's just empty. So, yeah, I guess I have completely lost interest. It's all just gone.
How long have you been feeling this way? Has it been at least two weeks, or has it been longer—maybe several months or more?

Well, doc, that's... see, that's the thing. Two weeks? No, no, it's been a lot longer than two weeks. I'd say... well, if I really sit down and trace it back, the heavy feeling, the... the whole depression part of it, it's been with me for about a year and two months now. Yeah, right around a year and two months. 

I know that sounds specific, but I can pin it down because it started not long after the move. We had to pack up the old place over on Elm Street—lived there for twelve years, had the garden exactly how I liked it, the tomatoes were finally coming in strong—and we moved into this smaller apartment complex closer to the campus. It made sense on paper, you know, shorter commute, less yard work, lower rent... but moving at my age, after fifteen years on the night shift, it just... it took something out of me. 

I remember it was a Tuesday, late October, when we finally got the last box unloaded. It was a box of kitchen stuff, mostly mugs and some old Tupperware. I set it on the counter, and I just stood there looking out the window at the parking lot of the new place. And that's when it hit me. That heavy, sinking feeling. I thought it was just exhaustion from hauling boxes up two flights of stairs, but... it never left. It just settled right into my bones. 

So through the winter, through the spring, right on through this past summer... it's just been this constant weight. I kept thinking, "Oh, it's just the winter blues, it'll pass when it warms up," or, "I'm just getting used to the new route at work." But here we are, fourteen months later, and I'm still sitting in that breakroom staring at the vending machine, feeling like I'm made of lead. So yeah, definitely not just two weeks. It's been a long, long year and some change.
